explanations.explanation: This neuron is a boundary‐detector: it spikes (strongly negative) on the very first or last token of a self‐contained text chunk (e.g. the opening word or the closing period of a sentence/paragraph).

This neuron fires on the “openers” of secondary descriptive/comparative phrases—i.e. on prepositions (with, to, for, as, like) and key verbs (wore, went, kept, qualified, etc.) that launch adjuncts of manner, role, comparison or purpose.

This neuron fires on the little “section‐header” or “step” markers that kick off list items, instructions or feature bullets—those one-word signals like Step, Then, Next, Now, Learn, Model, Make, Simply (and even descriptive lead-ins like Large) that demarcate new ordered steps, sections or feature entries in tutorials, how-tos, promotions and spec lists.

This neuron specializes in prepositional markers of rate or agency—firing on “per” in percentage phrases (“x per cent”) and on “by” introducing instrumental/causal clauses (“By clicking… you agree…”).

This neuron flags the “launch” of an attribute or qualifier phrase—i.e. function‐word cues (in, with, apart from, despite, known, featuring, so, etc.) that introduce supplementary descriptive or evaluative modifiers to the preceding text.

This feature is essentially a “named‐entity” detector at the subword level: it lights up whenever the model sees a chunk of a proper name, acronym, brand or technical term (including people’s names, place names, drug names, product model numbers, dates, measurements, etc.).

This neuron is a “Night” detector— it strongly activates on the token “Night” (and its use in compound names like “Night Shift,” “Night Sky,” “Night Safari,” etc.), flagging headings, event names, or feature titles that invoke “Night.”

This neuron fires on the kind of punchy, all-caps or title-style phrases you find at the top of sections, listicles, ads, or calls-to-action (e.g. “WHAT…,” “HOW…,” “BEST,” “MORE,” “ABOUT,” “SHOWHOUSE OPEN,” etc.)—in other words, it flags headline or subheading language rather than running prose.
This neuron lights up on second‐person, reader-directed language—especially “you” (and variants like “guys,” “ya”) in casual greetings, well-wishes, or thank-you/sign-off phrases.

This feature fires on the auxiliary “been” in perfect‐ and passive‐voice constructions (e.g. “has been revealed,” “has been added,” “has been shown”), marking statements of completed or newly reported actions.

This feature fires on markers of enumeration and quantification—words that express counts, measures or categories (numbers, quantifiers like “one,” “couple,” count nouns like “views,” “nominations,” “percent,” and category words like “types”/“kinds”).

This neuron reliably fires on the “root” of each high‐level clause or proposition—most often the finite verb (especially modals and auxiliaries like will, do/does, could) or, in noun‐headed questions or statements, the head noun (e.g. every, Investment, discover). In effect it marks the core predicate or subject of each sentence‐level unit.

This head is essentially a “named‐entity subtoken” detector: it lights up on the little BPE pieces that make up names—places, people, orgs, product or protein names, etc.—across languages and domains.

This feature fires on words that head prepositional/adverbial modifiers expressing temporal or conditional/basis relations—e.g. duration nouns (“hours,” “days,” “weeks”) and participial qualifiers (“based,” “dependent,” “relying,” “depending,” “focused,” “face-on,” “ultraviolet”) that introduce “when,” “why” or “on what basis” clauses.

This neuron appears to fire whenever a token is being used in a headline‐ or section‐header–style context—i.e. words that kick off titles or labels (infinitival “To,” calls-to-action like “Can” or “JUST,” part markers like “Part”/“Above,” promotional/opening verbs like “Follow,” etc.) rather than ordinary running text.

This neuron is not picking out any particular word meaning so much as structural “break” tokens in news‐style text—things that mark a shift into a new segment or embedded element (colons introducing quotes or lists, double‐dashes or parentheses for asides, and section‐style labels like “Video,” “star,” “Councillor,” etc.). In other words, it activates on formatting/structural cues rather than on topical content.

This neuron fires on “teaser” or “preview” language—discourse cues that promise an early look or outline what’s coming next (e.g. sneak-peek/preview, step-by-step, invitations to “come,” “face” what’s ahead, etc.).

This feature is essentially a “dot detector” – it spikes on the period token when it’s being used as a boundary marker (sentence-final full stop, decimal point or list/figure separator, and the dot in common abbreviations like “Inc.”, “St.”, “U.S.C.”, “M.D.”, etc.).
This neuron is basically flagging “word‐starts” – it lights up whenever a BPE piece comes right after whitespace/punctuation (i.e. the first subtoken of a new word).
This neuron is a sentence-boundary detector, firing strongly on the final “.” that marks the end of a sentence.
